title: Refuting the "Evil People Are the Primary Target" Doctrine
author: Zhanran
excerpt: A questioner has said: Though the offenses of an ordinary being are great, weighed against the power of the vows they are no more than a single grain in the vast sea (though the offenses of an ordinary being are great, compared with the power of Amitabha Buddha's vows they are as a single grain beside the ocean, utterly insignificant), and therefore breaking the precepts and doing evil do not matter at all.

inline.s: A questioner has said: Though the offenses of an ordinary being are great, weighed against the power of the vows they are no more than a single grain in the vast sea
(Though the offenses of an ordinary being are great, compared with the power of Amitabha Buddha's vows they are as a single grain beside the ocean, utterly insignificant)
, and therefore breaking the precepts and doing evil do not matter at all.
Answer: The power of Amitabha Buddha's vows is embodied in the Forty-eight Great Vows. Among them, the three vows that gather in living beings are these:
If, when I attain buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions
with sincere mind and joyful faith, aspiring to be born in my land, should say my Name even ten times
, and yet should not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Excluded are those who commit the five grave offenses and those who slander the true Dharma.
(the Eighteenth Vow)
If, when I attain buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions
should arouse the bodhi mind, cultivate all virtues, and with sincere mind make vows, aspiring to be born in my land
, and at the end of their lives I should fail to appear before them surrounded by a great assembly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(the Nineteenth Vow)
If, when I attain buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions, hearing my name
, should fix their thoughts on my land, plant roots of virtue, and with sincere mind dedicate the merit, aspiring to be born in my land
, and their wish should not be fulfilled, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(the Twentieth Vow)

Those who break the precepts and do evil not only fail to 'cultivate all virtues' and to 'plant roots of virtue' — they do the very opposite. They therefore do not meet the Nineteenth and Twentieth Vows. Do they then meet the Eighteenth Vow?
That depends on whether they can sustain ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life
(see
The Eighteenth Vow
for details)

Yet when their minds are scattered and they indulge themselves in ordinary times, will they be able to summon right mindfulness when the sufferings of death press in upon them? Will they be able to sustain ten consecutive thoughts? If they cannot — and if in life they kept no precepts but did evil instead — then after death the realm their consciousness enters will be determined by the karma of their broken precepts and their evil deeds.
Such cause, such fruit — this matters a very great deal.

So when people use the absurd logic that 'though the offenses of an ordinary being are great, weighed against the power of the vows they are no more than a single grain in the vast sea, and therefore breaking the precepts and doing evil do not matter at all' to incite others to break the precepts and do evil, the consequences are extremely grave:
they are leading the Buddha's disciples into a pit of fire!

The Original Vow school loudly proclaims that 'those who call the Name will surely be born' and the doctrine that 'evil people are the primary target,' and it slanderously claims that this is Master Shandao's Pure Land thought. The claim that 'those who call the Name will surely be born' turns up everywhere — in Master Jingzong's lecture series Master Shandao's Pure Land Thought, for instance. The same is true of the 'evil people are the primary target' doctrine: Master Huijing, for example, says in The Essentials of Master Shandao's Teaching, 'People do not realize that the purpose of the Contemplation Sutra is to make manifest Amitabha's original vow: evil people are the primary target.' Master Huijing's ordained disciple Master Xinyuan says in Amitabha's Deliverance Takes Evil People as Its Primary Target, 'Let us now consider: for what kind of beings does Amitabha Buddha's deliverance take as its primary target? Evil people are the primary target.'
In the chapter on the lowest grade of the lowest birth in the Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the World-Honored One teaches
that those who commit the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds,
by sustaining ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life
, thereby attain
the wiping away of their offenses
and rebirth, their grade being the lowest of the nine grades of birth.
The sutra text reads as follows:

"The Buddha said to Ānanda and Vaidehi: The lowest grade of the lowest birth concerns those sentient beings who commit unwholesome deeds, the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds, and are possessed of every kind of unwholesomeness. Because of these evil deeds, such a foolish person ought to fall into the evil realms and, passing through many kalpas, endure suffering without end. When such a foolish person is about to die, he meets a good teacher who comforts him in various ways, expounds the wondrous Dharma for him, and teaches him to be mindful of the Buddha. But that person, oppressed by suffering, has no leisure to be mindful of the Buddha, and the good friend tells him: 'If you cannot be mindful of that Buddha, then you should call upon the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and take refuge in him.'
Thus, with a sincere mind, keeping the voice unbroken, he completes ten thoughts, reciting 'Namo Amitabha Buddha'

. Because he calls the Buddha's name, with each thought he erases the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eight billion kalpas. At the moment of death, he sees a golden lotus flower like the disk of the sun come to rest before him, and in the time of a single thought he is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. For twelve great kalpas he remains within the lotus flower, and only then does the flower open. When it opens, Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with voices of great compassion, expound for him the Dharma of true reality and the eradication of offenses; hearing it, he rejoices and at once arouses the mind of bodhi. This is called the lowest grade of the lowest birth. This is called the contemplation of the lowest class of beings, and it is the sixteenth contemplation."
(for annotations, see
Notes on the Chapter on the Lowest Grade of the Lowest Birth in the Contemplation Sutra
for details)
In his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles, Master Shandao explains the meaning of this chapter (the chapter on the lowest grade of the lowest birth) as follows:

"From 'such a foolish person' down to 'the offenses of birth and death,' the passage sets forth precisely how one who hears the Dharma and recites the Buddha's name receives benefit in the present, and this contains ten points: 1. It restates the person who committed evil; 2. It shows that his remaining life is short; 3. It shows that at the end of life he meets a good teacher; 4. It shows the good person comforting him and teaching him to recite the Buddha's name; 5. It shows that the sinner, pressed by the suffering of death, has no way to recite the Buddha's name; 6. It shows the good friend, knowing his suffering and loss of mindfulness, turning to teach him to call Amitabha's name with his mouth; 7. It shows the number of recitations,
each sound unbroken
; 8. It shows the eradication of offenses over many kalpas; 9. It shows
that with right mindfulness at the end of life, a golden lotus immediately appears in response
; 10. It shows the speed of his departure, going straight to the land of his destination."
Note especially what Master Shandao says in his exposition: "
each sound unbroken
" and "
with right mindfulness at the end of life, a golden lotus comes to welcome him
." Join these with Master Shandao's statements that 'continuity of thought brings rebirth' and that there must be 'right mindfulness at the end of life' (see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
for details), and the meaning of these two phrases becomes even clearer:
the thoughts of Buddha-recitation at the end of life continue without interruption
(unmixed with deluded thoughts)
, and one attains rebirth.
And we know clearly that Master Shandao says in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles,
"If one can do so for a whole lifetime at most, or for as few as ten thoughts at least, then by the power of the Buddha's vow none fail to be reborn — hence it is called easy,"
and
says in the Hymns of Praise for Rebirth,
"If I attain buddhahood and the sentient beings of the ten directions who call my name, even as few as ten times, are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment,"
and that in these passages 'as few as ten thoughts'
means ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life

. Yet the Original Vow school distorts it to mean any ten thoughts whatsoever, and so draws the conclusion: Master Shandao taught that those who call the Name will surely be born! (see Master Jingzong's lecture series Master Shandao's Pure Land Thought for details)

Moreover, Master Shandao's statement in the Hymns of Praise for Rebirth — 'If I attain buddhahood and the sentient beings of the ten directions who call my name, even as few as ten times, are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment' — comes from the Eighteenth Vow in the Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Immeasurable Life

"If, when I attain buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions, with sincere mind and joyful faith, aspiring to be born in my land, should say my Name even ten times, and yet should not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Excluded are those who commit the five grave offenses and those who slander the true Dharma."
The phrase 'even ten times' in the Eighteenth Vow means
ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life,
as the patriarchs and great masters of the Pure Land school through the ages have analyzed with complete clarity (see
The Eighteenth Vow

for details). How then could Master Shandao's 'as few as ten thoughts' possibly mean that those who call the Name will surely be born — that any ten thoughts at any ordinary time will certainly bring rebirth?
Moreover, throughout his life Master Shandao upheld
"continuity of thought brings rebirth"
(see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching

for details), and Master Yinguang praised this without stint: 'Its benefit is boundless!' How can anyone say that Master Shandao upheld the view that those who call the Name will surely be born? Quite the contrary: what Master Shandao upheld was
"continuity of thought brings rebirth"!
Moreover, as quoted above, Master Shandao states unmistakably in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles:
with right mindfulness at the end of life
, a golden lotus comes to welcome him."
This means that rebirth comes about because there is
right mindfulness at the end of life
. How can anyone say that Master Shandao upheld the view that those who call the Name will surely be born? Quite the contrary: what Master Shandao upheld was
"right mindfulness at the end of life"!
Moreover, in Master Shandao's Text on Right Mindfulness at the End of Life for Rebirth, Master Shandao sets it out with perfect clarity:
one must have right mindfulness at the end of life in order to attain rebirth
(see
Notes on Master Shandao's Text on Right Mindfulness at the End of Life for Rebirth
for details). Since right mindfulness at the end of life is indispensable for rebirth, how can it be that those who call the Name will surely be born?

Originally, the chapter on the lowest grade of the lowest birth in the Contemplation Sutra teaches that the grade of such a person — one who has achieved ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life, eradicated offenses, and attained rebirth, though a committer of the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds — is the lowest grade of the lowest birth,
but the Original Vow school deliberately omits
ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life,

this crucial point, and exaggerates it into the claim that all who commit the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds attain rebirth, and proclaims 'those who call the Name will surely be born' along with the so-called 'evil people are the primary target' doctrine. Master Huijing says in The Essentials of Master Shandao's Teaching, 'People do not realize that the purpose of the Contemplation Sutra is to make manifest Amitabha's original vow: evil people are the primary target.' Master Huijing's ordained disciple Master Xinyuan says, 'Let us now consider: for what kind of beings does Amitabha Buddha's deliverance take as its primary target? Evil people are the primary target.'

Yet even those who commit the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds and attain rebirth, as the sutra describes, do so because in past lives they deeply planted roots of virtue and once sowed the seeds of bodhi. Master Ouyi
says
"The sutra says that those who commit the ten evil deeds and the five grave offenses attain rebirth
because in the past they must have sown the seeds of bodhi

. Without the seeds of bodhi, how could they meet a good friend? And even meeting a good friend who urges and inspires them, how could they at once give rise to faith and vows and recite the great Name?"
(Lingfeng's Collected Discourses, 'Universal Instruction at Tianma Cloister, Shepu')
Master Ouyi also says:
"As for the ten thoughts at the end of life,
one must have deeply planted roots of virtue

. If today, when adverse or favorable conditions arise, one no longer has right mindfulness, how much less at the end of life? Moreover, when the suffering of death appears, one can rely only on a good friend's prompting; yet now, under a clear sky and bright sun, one still cannot accept and practice the true words of a clear teacher and good friend!"
(Lingfeng's Collected Discourses
'Preface to the Pure Land Repentance and Life-Release Society')
(Translation

: To accomplish the ten thoughts at the end of life, one must have deeply planted roots of virtue. If today, when adverse or favorable conditions come, one no longer has right mindfulness, how much less will one be able to keep right mindfulness at the end of life? Furthermore, if today, under a clear sky and bright sun, one cannot accept and practice the true admonitions of a clear teacher and good friend, can one really imagine that when the suffering of death appears, mere reliance on a good friend's reminders and instruction will enable one to accept and practice them?)
Evil people are the primary target" is utterly mistaken. The basis of Pure Land study and practice is the three Pure Land sutras; let us see what these three sutras say:
In the Buddha Speaks the Amitabha Sutra, the Buddha says:
It is not by scant roots of virtue and blessings and causal conditions
(that is, one may not attain it by slight causes and conditions of roots of virtue and blessings)
that one may attain birth in that land
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)

[Roots of virtue]: the goodness of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because it can produce wondrous fruit, it is called a root. [Sentient beings]: also called living beings, that is, all creatures possessed of sentience and consciousness.
In the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says:
Those who wish to be born in that land
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
should cultivate three blessings
: First, to be filial to and support one's parents, to serve and honor one's teachers, to be compassionate and refrain from killing,
and to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds
; Second, to receive and uphold the three refuges,
to observe all the precepts fully,
and to violate none of the rules of deportment; Third, to arouse the mind of bodhi,
to deeply believe in cause and effect
, to read and recite the Mahayana scriptures, and to encourage others to advance. These three things are called pure karma."
(see
Notes on the Chapter on the Lowest Grade of the Lowest Birth in the Contemplation Sutra
for details)

In the Buddha Speaks the Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha devotes many passages to teaching the observance of precepts and the ending of evil and the practice of good. For example:
"You should resolutely decide for yourselves,
rectify your bodies and conduct, and increasingly do what is good
Cultivate yourselves and purify your bodies; wash away the defilements of the mind
Let your words and deeds be loyal and trustworthy,
your outward manner corresponding to your inner state. One can save oneself, and then in turn save others; with clear understanding make your vows,
accumulate the roots of goodness
. Though you labor diligently for a single lifetime, in an instant,
you will be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with joy beyond all limit
"You should reflect on this deeply,
keep far from all evil, choose what is good, and diligently practice it
You gods and people of the present, and people of future generations, who obtain the Buddha's sutra words, should reflect on them deeply and, in accordance with them,
rectify your minds and conduct
Each of you should consider this well and teach and admonish one another,
in accordance with the Buddha's sutras and Dharma, committing no transgression
"The world being thus, the Buddha pities all beings. By his awesome spiritual power he destroys all evil
and causes all to turn toward goodness
. Cast away your thoughts,
uphold the sutras and precepts,

receive and practice the Dharma, failing in nothing, and in the end attain the way of nirvana that saves one from the world." "You gods and people of the present, and people of future generations, who obtain the Buddha's sutra words, should reflect on them deeply and, in accordance with them,
rectify your minds and conduct
Let rulers do good
and lead and transform those below them, instructing one another in turn,
each keeping to what is right
Honor the sages, respect the good; be kind, compassionate, and universally loving
Do not dare to fail or betray the Buddha's words and instructions

. You should seek to be saved from the world, to uproot the source of all evil in birth and death, and to depart from the path of the three evil realms with its immeasurable sorrow, fear, and suffering. In this way you
broadly plant the roots of virtue,
bestow kindness and confer benefits,
and transgress none of the Dharma's prohibitions
Practice patience and diligence, single-mindedness and wisdom. Teach and transform one another; establish virtue and do good. Rectify your minds and thoughts; keep the precepts pure.
Do not follow your own desires at will, betraying the sutras and precepts and falling behind others.

Yet the Original Vow school turns its back on the three Pure Land sutras, using the 'evil people are the primary target' doctrine to incite the breaking of precepts and the doing of evil, corrupting the fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople, and above all seeking to destroy the true Sangha, the teachers of gods and humans. This is the destruction of the Buddha's true Dharma!
The Buddha said:
"The future destruction of the true Dharma will not come from the attacks of heavenly demons and outside paths, but precisely from the corruption and collapse of the Sangha!"
(On the Treasures of the Sangha)

Consider: those disciples and believers who are bewitched by this 'those who call the Name will surely be born' and this 'evil people are the primary target' doctrine neither recite the Buddha's name with diligent single-mindedness, nor, believing in 'evil people are the primary target,' cease evil and practice good — some even do evil their whole lives (including slandering the true Dharma). Do they have the merit and the spiritual strength to sustain ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life? If they cannot, where will they go after death, and what will their karmic reward be in life after life to come?
The enormous harm of the 'evil people are the primary target' doctrine lies in this:
1. Its victims and their families suffer extreme pain;
2. Social order is disturbed and undermined;
3. The image of Buddhism and of the Buddha's disciples is gravely damaged;
4. The evildoers themselves not only fail to attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but also suffer grievous retribution.

[Evildoers themselves not only fail to attain rebirth but also suffer grievous retribution.] Because the Buddha-Dharma is the true Dharma, an evil mind can never be in accord with it. Adherents of the 'evil people are the primary target' doctrine can test themselves: setting aside the moment of death, even when ordinary conditions arise in daily life, can they keep their mindfulness clear (ten consecutive thoughts)? Since they cannot attain rebirth, they will certainly suffer grievous retribution according to the evil karma they have created.
For many years Master Huijing has spared no effort in loudly promoting the Original Vow school, and
in his promotion of the 'evil people are the primary target' doctrine
he has been especially painstaking,
openly and slanderously declaring that taking evil people as the primary target is Amitabha Buddha's original vow
. In The Essentials of Master Shandao's Teaching he says:
"People do not realize that the purpose of the Contemplation Sutra
is to make manifest Amitabha's original vow
evil people are the primary target
Moreover, he especially
selected 'essential Dharma words' from The Complete Works of Master Honen and compiled them into Master Honen's
Forty-eight
Dharma Words (also titled Dharma Words on Peace of Mind through Buddha-Recitation), which he bills as 'Dharma words of Buddha-recitation that set the mind at peace.' In the opening he writes:
Master Honen

"founded the Japanese Pure Land school on the Pure Land thought of Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitabha. Master Honen received the very marrow of Master Shandao's mind and entered the Pure Land school through Master Shandao's 'passage on the definitely assured karma.'"
In fact, this collection of Dharma Words runs wholly counter to the sutras and treatises, and wholly counter to Master Shandao's teaching.
In these Dharma Words, Master Honen says:
"The
essential heart
of the Pure Land school is this: no matter who one is, whoever recites the Buddha's name will attain rebirth. Even for the most wicked person in the world, one without equal
(beyond all comparison)
, if he recites Namo Amitabha Buddha, then even a single thought brings rebirth."
Look! This is the
essential heart
of the Original Vow school: the worst evildoer in the world
(an evildoer without equal)

, merely by reciting the Buddha's name once, attains rebirth. With these Dharma Words on Peace of Mind in hand, those who stop at no evil have nothing to fear! In the Buddha Speaks the Amitabha Sutra, the Buddha says:
"One cannot attain birth in that land with few roots of virtue, blessings, and causal conditions."

Yet Master Honen openly proclaims that one need only recite the Buddha's name once, and then may do any evil deed whatsoever, for in the end one will be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and enjoy every pleasure forever. Is this the Buddha-Dharma? They also loudly proclaim that 'evil people are the primary target' and slanderously claim that this is 'Amitabha's original vow.'
Master Honen also says in these Dharma Words:
"If a person commits the five grave offenses

(the five grave offenses: five evils utterly contrary to principle — killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, shedding the Buddha's blood, and disrupting the harmonious Sangha. These five are acts of extreme evil; committing any one of them brings a fall into the unintermitted hell, and so they are also called 'unintermitted karma')
, and hears the six-character name
(hears 'Namo Amitabha Buddha')
, the fiery cart departs of itself
(the fiery cart of hell departs of itself)
, and the lotus throne comes at once to welcome him."

This is nothing less than incitement to evil! Such incitement means that those who follow it not only fail to attain rebirth after death but must go to the evil realms to receive retribution; and the disruption of society, the damage to Buddhism, and the harm done to others are all most severe.
As for the teaching of cause and effect — 'good deeds bring good rewards, evil deeds bring evil rewards' —

Master Yinguang teaches in the Preface to Evidential Records of Cause and Effect that the sages of the world and the sages beyond the world govern the realm, bring peace to society, and deliver living beings by the great sovereign power of
karmic retribution
The Buddhist sutras explain the karmic retribution of the three periods of time most exhaustively. To put it in brief:
If you would know the causes past, look at what this life receives; if you would know the fruits to come, look at what this life achieves.
(original text:

"Cause and effect is the great sovereign power by which the sages of the world and beyond the world govern the realm, bring peace to society, and deliver living beings. ... The Buddhist sutras explain the cause and effect of the three periods of time most exhaustively. To put it in brief: If you would know the causes past, look at what this life receives; if you would know the fruits to come, look at what this life achieves."

Therefore the teaching of cause and effect — of reward for good and evil — is of the utmost importance! It leads people to cease evil and practice good, so that they escape evil retribution and obtain good rewards, and thereby governs the realm, brings peace to society, and delivers living beings.
Master Yinguang therefore promoted the teaching of cause and effect with all his strength, and he taught:
"Cause and effect is the great sovereign power by which the sages of the world and beyond the world govern the realm, bring peace to society, and deliver living beings. For
(because)

if cause and effect is not promoted, then good cannot be encouraged nor evil punished; only the greatly worthy can keep to their place and follow the Way — as for the rest, who would not wish to give free rein to their hearts and take their pleasure in this one life?" "
When everyone knows cause and effect, that is the way of great order; when no one knows cause and effect, that is the way of great chaos.
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
'Preface to Selected Notes of Lord Ji Wenda')
"Morality, righteousness, and benevolence are the inherent virtue of our nature;
karmic retribution is truly the great sovereign power of heaven and earth in their transforming nurture

." "If people knew karmic retribution, then good and evil, calamity and blessing, would be as clear as fire in the dark — who would not wish to seek good fortune and avoid misfortune, to escape calamity and gain blessing?"
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
'A Treatise on Turning Back the Kalpa of Calamity, Protecting the Nation, Saving the People, and Returning to the Root and Cleansing the Source')

Yet the Original Vow school proclaims that 'evil people are the primary target,' turning the law of karmic retribution — 'good deeds bring good rewards, evil deeds bring evil rewards' — upside down and confounding living beings. It incites people, saying: evil brings no evil retribution but rather great blessing; you need only recite the Buddha's name once, and you may then go ahead and do any wicked thing at all, for after death you will go straight to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to enjoy every pleasure forever, because
evil people
are the very
primary target
of Amitabha Buddha's deliverance (during the war of aggression against China, the military chaplains of the Japanese Original Vow school incited Japanese soldiers in exactly this way; see
The Practice of Master Honen's Teaching
! Evil
(including the five grave offenses)
brings no evil retribution but instead great blessing — a single recitation of the Buddha's name has become a talisman for doing evil!
This
wholly contradicts the Buddhist sutras, violates the causal law of retribution for good and evil, destroys the teaching of cause and effect, and incites people's minds toward evil.

When you read such devilish talk, does it set your mind at ease? As disciples of the Buddha, we should not merely refrain from spreading these wicked falsehoods — we should denounce them in speech and in writing, in order to protect the Buddha's true Dharma.

This means: a great evildoer who has committed the five grave offenses need only hear the Buddha's name — without even reciting it — and he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to enjoy every pleasure forever. If that were really so, what evil deed would anyone in the world still fear to commit? Does this accord with reality? Is this how the Buddha-Dharma teaches and transforms living beings?
As for how
one may attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss,
Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitabha Buddha, speaks with perfect clarity
(see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
for details)
It is precisely because calling the Name is easy that
continuity of thought brings rebirth
. If one can
continue thought after thought
with one's whole life as the term
then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.
May all people reflect well on this: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
discipline the mind and master
to spur oneself on and restrain oneself
never slackening day or night,
so that as the former thought ends, the next thought is born.
Forever enjoying the Dharma-bliss of the unconditioned, and at last attaining buddhahood — is that not wonderful!

Master Shandao was an emanation of Amitabha Buddha; his words are Amitabha Buddha's words. How one may attain rebirth must of course rest upon his words as its authority! Those who recite the Buddha's name must engrave this on their hearts, believing yet more deeply, and trusting yet more firmly.
Yet this Honen says the very opposite: where is there any need for 'continuity of thought brings rebirth'? Where is there any need for 'disciplining the mind and mastering oneself'? Even if
a great evildoer who has committed the five grave offenses
('if a person commits the five grave offenses')
need only hear the Buddha's name
('hears the six-character name')
to be at once reborn
('the fiery cart departs of itself, the lotus throne comes at once to welcome him')
Is this really
relying on
the Pure Land thought of Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitabha"? Is this really "
receiving
the very marrow of Master Shandao's mind"
From the above we can see that Master Shandao taught
"continuity of thought brings rebirth"
and
"disciplining the mind and mastering oneself"
, while Master Honen, in direct opposition, loudly proclaims
that "those who call the Name will surely be born
(indeed, even those who merely hear the Name will surely be born)
and
that "evil people are the primary target

(he proclaims: not only is there no need to discipline the mind and master oneself, but one may do any wicked thing at will — kill one's father, kill one's mother, kill an arhat, shed the Buddha's blood, disrupt the harmonious Sangha, all of it! — 'the fiery cart departs of itself, the lotus throne comes at once to welcome him.')
"Those who call the Name will surely be born"
and
"evil people are the primary target"
— these two are the
essential heart
It cleverly exploits the weaknesses of human nature — the fear of hardship, the wish for an easy shortcut, the craving for worldly pleasures — in order to deceive believers.

"Those who call the Name will surely be born" is the theoretical justification for monastics not needing to practice; "evil people are the primary target" is the theoretical justification for monastics not needing to keep the precepts or to cease evil and practice good. And so monastics degenerate from practitioners of the Way into professional monks who neither keep precepts nor practice — growing their hair, eating meat, taking wives, doing evil, anything at all. The tragedy is that they still believe they will certainly attain rebirth, since they have 'those who call the Name will surely be born' and 'evil people are the primary target' as their guarantees — never realizing that these are nothing but deceitful devil's talk! See
The Original Vow School Is an Outside Path Attached to Buddhism
and
The Practice of Master Honen's Teaching
“Reciting the Name assures rebirth” and “the wicked one as the true subject”
are the two points that form the heart-essence of the Primal Vow Dharma-gate] This is what Master Hōnen himself said. Hōnen said:
The heart-essence of the
Pure Land school
lies in this: whoever it may be, anyone who recites the Buddha’s name attains rebirth.
Even a wicked person without peer
(unmatchable)
in the world
, if he recites Namo Amitābha Buddha,
will attain rebirth even with a single thought
This not only fails to grasp the heart-essence of Master Shandao, but deliberately
falsified
the Pure Land thought of Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha, in order to establish the Primal Vow Dharma-gate
. For eight hundred years, who knows how many reciters it has misled in their wisdom-life!
Q: Master Daochuo said:

“If any sentient being, even if he commits evil throughout his life, at the moment of death continues ten recitations, calling upon my name, and is not reborn, then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

Since it says “even if one commits evil throughout one’s life,” as long as “at the moment of death the ten recitations continue,” one is certain to attain rebirth, so does that mean a reciter need not abandon evil and practice good? Is this so?
A:
“Even if one commits evil throughout one’s life, as long as at the moment of death the ten recitations continue, one is certain to attain rebirth”

indicates that right mindfulness at the moment of death, the continuation of the ten recitations, is of the utmost importance. That is to say, the continuity of the ten recitations at death is the sole requirement for rebirth; as long as the ten recitations continue at the moment of death, one can induce Amitābha Buddha to come and guide one across.

But to reach this requirement, one must in daily life accomplish the habit of continuing the ten recitations until it becomes second nature, and abandoning evil and practicing good are extremely important auxiliary conditions. Therefore Master Shandao taught:
“May all people reflect well within themselves; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
one must exert one’s mind and restrain oneself,

abandoning not a single moment day or night. When the previous thought reaches life’s end, the next thought is rebirth. Forever enjoying the unconditioned joy of the Dharma, and on up to Buddhahood, how delightful that would be!”
The
“exert one’s mind and restrain oneself”

of which he spoke means to spur oneself on and to discipline oneself. A person who indulges himself and commits evil cannot achieve “exerting the mind and restraining oneself,” and is moreover out of accord with single-minded recitation free of confused thoughts.
On this, the Repentance Master Ciyun (Zunshi) taught:

“Thus, when one fixes one’s mind on the Buddha, spontaneously and constantly it of itself blocks all evil thoughts. If one is about to do evil, because one recollects the Buddha, the evil cannot come to be.”
The Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Making the Vow of Rebirth in the Pure Land

Therefore, a person who does not exert his mind and restrain himself finds it hard to accomplish the habit of continuing the ten recitations until it becomes second nature, so the continuity of the ten recitations at death is not assured. Conversely, if one truly accomplishes the habit of continuing the ten recitations until it becomes second nature, one will not go on committing evil, because
“if one is about to do evil, because one recollects the Buddha, the evil cannot come to be”

There are also extremely rare exceptions in which one commits evil throughout one’s life and yet accomplishes “at the moment of death, the continuation of the ten recitations.” Such a case is that of a cultivator who, in a former life, already possessed considerable attainment, but because he had not completely cut off the delusions of view and thought, transmigrated into this life. In this life he again strayed onto a wrong path and committed evil throughout his life. At the moment of death, awakened by the instruction of a good friend, he repented with all his heart and accomplished the continuation of the ten recitations and was reborn. Consider: if it were not based upon the bodhi-mind and the profound attainment of a former life, how, amid the pressing together of all the miseries at the moment of death, could he suddenly give rise to faith and vows and abruptly accomplish the continuation of the ten recitations?

Therefore one must never imitate this, for among ten thousand people reborn in the Pure Land, hardly one is such a case. Consider: if one normally indulges one’s conduct and lets the mind do evil, and when adverse or favorable conditions arise the mind follows them away, then amid the pressing together of all the miseries at the moment of death, how could one accomplish the continuation of the ten recitations? On this principle, since ancient times the great masters and venerable ancestors have given many, many teachings and discussions.
